intro: Thailand has more than 130 national parks, and each one charges entrance fees under roughly the same system run by the Department of National Parks, Wildlife and Plant Conservation — the actual numbers just vary by how popular and how large the park is. This page collects entrance fees for the parks people visit most often into one table, explains how the pricing system works, then points you to the full guide for each one.
quickAnswerHtml: Most Thai national parks charge two prices — Thai adults pay roughly 40–100 baht (show a Thai ID for this rate; seniors and people with disabilities usually enter free), and foreign adults pay roughly 200–400 baht, depending on how well-known the park is. Popular parks like Khao Yai charge the most, at 400 baht. Park accommodation needs to be booked ahead through nps.dnp.go.th.
quickAnswerH2: Thailand national park fees, decided in one line

blocks.html: Short answer: almost every Thai national park uses a two-tier pricing system — Thai visitors pay 3–5 times less than foreign visitors — and vehicles are usually charged separately from people. Most tickets are valid only for the day they were bought, though a few parks let you re-enter on the same ticket if you're staying overnight inside. Below is a comparison table for the six most-visited parks, followed by how the pricing system works and how to book accommodation.

items: Two-tier pricing: Thai visitors always pay less than foreigners — just show a Thai ID card or Thai passport at the ticket counter, no other documents needed.
Kids, seniors, disabilities: Children usually pay half price. Thai seniors aged 60+ and visitors with disabilities enter free at most major parks — bring an ID or senior card.
Vehicles cost extra: Cars, motorbikes and buses have a separate entry fee on top of the per-person fee, and it varies by vehicle size and by park.
Tickets are single-day: Most tickets expire once you leave the park that day, except at a few parks that allow re-entry on the same ticket if you don't leave the area overnight.

Special sites cost more: Some landmarks inside a park charge an extra fee on top of the standard entrance — for example, the twin pagodas on Doi Inthanon charge extra beyond the regular park entrance fee.

blocks.title: Most parks close during the rainy season
blocks.html: Some trails (like the Kew Mae Pan trail on Doi Inthanon) and mountaintop parks like Phu Kradueng usually close from June to September or October to let the forest recover and to prevent landslide danger. Always check each park's open season before planning, especially if you're traveling in the rainy months.

blocks.text: How to book national park accommodation

blocks.html: Many parks have their own bungalows and camping grounds you can book directly, separate from hotels outside the park. Park-run rooms and rental tents fill up fast around long weekends and high season, so book at least 2–4 weeks ahead.

items: Book through the official site — the national booking system for park accommodation nationwide is at nps.dnp.go.th, covering both bungalows and rental tents.
Bring your own tent — cheapest option; you just pay a camping-ground fee, typically a few dozen baht per person per night, but you need to bring your own tent and sleeping gear.
Rent a park tent — no need to carry your own gear; rental tents at the main camping area typically run 225–600 baht a night depending on size.
Park bungalows — the most comfortable option, priced from a few hundred to several thousand baht per unit; book ahead since availability is limited.

faq.q: How much do Thai national parks charge for entry?
faq.a: It varies by park. Thai visitors typically pay 40–100 baht, while foreign visitors pay roughly 200–400 baht. Well-known, heavily visited parks like Khao Yai tend to charge the most. Check the sign at the park entrance or the Department of National Parks website for the current rate before you go.

faq.q: Why do Thai and foreign visitors pay different prices?
faq.a: It's a nationwide two-tier pricing policy used at almost every national park, not something specific to a few places. Foreign visitors typically pay 3–5 times more than Thai visitors. Show a Thai ID card or Thai passport at the counter to get the Thai rate.

faq.q: Can I book national park accommodation in advance?
faq.a: Yes, through the official Department of National Parks website at nps.dnp.go.th, which covers both bungalows and rental tents. Book at least 2–4 weeks ahead around long weekends, since park accommodation is limited and fills up fast.

faq.q: When are Thailand's national parks closed?
faq.a: Many parks close certain trails or the entire park during the rainy season (June to September or October) for safety and to let the forest recover — Phu Kradueng, for example, closes entirely during this period. Always check the specific park's open season before planning your trip.
